claims.statement: The axum server is built in `server::main` around an `AppState` of exactly three clones — the `SqlitePool`, a `broadcast::Sender<SseMessage>` with capacity 100, and a `CancellationToken` — and the GraphQL schema `Schema::build(QueryRoot, Mutation, EmptySubscription)` carries that pool, the broadcast sender and three DataLoaders in its context data. GraphQL declares no subscription type; long-running progress is delivered over `/events` instead.

The router is a fixed table on one `TcpListener`: `POST /graphql`, `GET /events`, `POST /dats|/roms|/patches|/irds` each with `DefaultBodyLimit::disable()`, `GET /romfiles/{id}`, `/mcp` nested as a service, and a `/{*path}` catch-all serving rust-embed assets with `/` serving `index.html`. Address defaults to `127.0.0.1` and port to `8000`.

The `CorsLayer` allowing any origin, method and header is installed only under `#[cfg(debug_assertions)]`, so a release server sends no CORS headers and requires the page and the API to share an origin; `frontend/Trunk.toml` reproduces that in dev by proxying `/graphql`, `/events`, `/dats` and `/romfiles/` to `127.0.0.1:8000`.

The SPA is compiled into the binary from `target/assets` via rust-embed; `build.rs` runs `trunk build --release` when the `server` feature is on unless `SKIP_TRUNK=true`, and still creates the assets directory so a build without a UI yields a working API with a missing UI rather than a compile failure. `serve_asset` sniffs the MIME type from the bytes, falls back to the extension, then to `application/octet-stream`, and returns an empty 404 for unknown paths.

A `server` or `mcp` build opens a five-connection SQLite pool with `PRAGMA locking_mode = NORMAL`, WAL and a 5-second `acquire_timeout`, where a headless CLI build opens a single connection with `EXCLUSIVE` locking; that five-connection budget is what spawned long-running actions contend against.

`IdLoader<T>` over the `TableRow` trait (TABLE, SELECT, row_id) batches the ids async-graphql collects per level into one `SELECT ... WHERE id in (...)`, and `Rom::game`, `Rom::romfile` and `Game::system` resolve through `load_one` rather than querying, so nested ROM/game/system selections cost one query per edge instead of one per row.

`System`'s `TableRow::SELECT` must enumerate the `games_complete` and `games_total` count subqueries because they are computed columns absent from `*`; if they drift from the equivalent subqueries in `database.rs`, rows loaded through `SystemLoader` fail to map even though the CLI path is unaffected. The ids interpolated into the loader's `IN` list are `i64`s already read from the database, not client input.

The four size aggregates (`totalOriginalSize`, `oneRegionOriginalSize`, `totalActualSize`, `oneRegionActualSize`) all funnel through `system_size`, which builds raw SQL: `actual` sums distinct `romfiles.size` (what is on disk) versus `roms.size` (the catalog figure), and `one_region` splices in `AND g.sorting = 1`. `Rom::ignored(systemId)` similarly mixes DataLoader lookups with one raw parent-`bios` query only for arcade systems that have a parent.

Response payload size is deliberately trimmed: `Game::description` returns `null` when it would only repeat `name` (the raw field is `graphql(skip)`ped), and `games(systemId, offset, limit)` pages a large system via `find_games_by_system_id_paged`, falling back to the unpaged query when `limit` is omitted.

Request-path mutations never panic on pool exhaustion: `acquire_connection` maps a failed `pool.acquire()` onto a typed `async_graphql::Error`, plain HTTP handlers answer `unavailable(e)` as 503, and spawned actions emit `{prefix}_error` over SSE rather than hanging. Query resolvers are the documented exception — most of `query.rs` still `unwrap()`s on acquire.

`spawn_cli_action` is one template for `sort_roms`, `check_roms`, `generate_playlists`, `purge_roms`, `convert_roms` and `purge_irds`: it spawns a task, emits `{prefix}_started` *before* acquiring a connection, then runs the CLI subcommand's own `main()` through a synthesised `ArgMatches` on a hidden progress bar, and closes with `{prefix}_complete` or `{prefix}_error`. `purge_system` and `download_dats` inline the same shape without the helper.

Because actions are requested from a browser with no TTY, mutations pre-answer every prompt a CLI run would raise — `-y` for `sort-roms` and `purge-roms`, `-u first` for `import-roms` — and give every action `ProgressBar::hidden()`.

Mutations that cannot possibly run are refused on the request path before anything is queued: an unknown `system_id` returns `System {id} not found`, `purgeRoms` with all four flags false returns `No ROM files selected to purge`, an unsupported convert format lists the valid ones, and `setPreferFormat` rejects a format the target arcade system cannot hold.

`src/validator.rs` supplies `VariantValidator<E>` over `strum::VariantNames` (region, version, subfolder scheme) plus `PreferFormatValidator` against `convert_roms::ALL_FORMATS` and `DirectoryValidator`, which canonicalises the path and requires an existing directory. Attached via `#[graphql(validator(custom = ...))]`, they reject bad values as input-value errors before any resolver body or database write.

All four upload endpoints accept multipart, skip unknown fields with a debug log instead of erroring, and return 202 Accepted as soon as the work is queued — outcome and progress arrive only over SSE. They differ in landing and pre-checks: `/dats` buffers bytes and writes a temp dir inside the task, `/roms` takes `file` or `url` plus `system`/`unattended`, `/patches` and `/irds` stream to a temp dir and resolve the target ROM/system first so a bad id is a 400 rather than a doomed background task.

`/roms`, `/patches` and `/irds` write multipart fields chunk-by-chunk into a fresh `tempfile::TempDir` instead of buffering, and the `TempDir` is deliberately carried alongside the path (`RomSource::Upload`, and the `directory` binding in the patch/IRD tasks) because dropping it deletes the file still being imported.

`/roms` accepts a `url` field that the **server** fetches, not the browser — so it can reach anything the server can, including its own private network, which the source comments and README flag as acceptable only for the default loopback bind. The in-code mitigations are a http/https scheme allow-list, a 30-second connect timeout, `error_for_status()`, and a 100 GiB cap enforced while streaming (`MAX_ROM_DOWNLOAD_SIZE`).

Client-chosen names are treated as untrusted: `safe_filename` keeps only the last non-empty, non-`.`/`..` segment split on both separators and falls back to `download`, and `url_filename` strips query/fragment and scheme/authority, percent-decodes, and then re-runs that same sanitiser — so `%2E%2E%2F%2E%2E%2Fetc%2Fpasswd` lands as `passwd`.

`download_romfile` reads the `ROM_DIRECTORY` setting, joins the `romfiles.path` row onto it and streams the file out as `application/octet-stream` with an `attachment` disposition; a missing setting or null value is 500, and a file that cannot be opened is 404 — but `find_romfile_by_id` panics for a nonexistent id.

`/events` forwards `SseMessage { event, data }` from the broadcast channel with keep-alives: a lagging subscriber is logged and skipped rather than disconnected, a closed channel or a cancelled token ends the stream, and `sse_send` silently drops messages when there is no subscriber or the channel is full. Progress bars are not bridged — only lifecycle events and their `message` cross SSE.

Because `EventSource` reconnects without replaying, the SPA resets its in-flight action flags on every `onopen` and clears each one on *either* `{prefix}_complete` or `{prefix}_error`; every `{prefix}_*` event name emitted by the server therefore has a matching listener, which makes emitting exactly one terminal event per action a hard contract.

The server has no authentication or authorisation: `/mcp` is nested on the same listener at the same trust level as `/graphql`, and `mcp_http_service` constructs its handler with `read_only = false`, so the mutating MCP tools are live over HTTP with no bearer token, as the README warns.

MCP's `run_action` mirrors the GraphQL action path — pooled connection, process-wide write lock, hidden progress bar — and when mounted on the web server it fans the same `{prefix}_started` / `_complete` / `_error` events into the SSE broadcast, so MCP-triggered work is visible to a browser watching `/events`.

Shutdown waits on Ctrl+C or SIGTERM, then runs `optimize_database(pool)` (incremental_vacuum, optimize, wal_checkpoint(truncate)) and only afterwards calls `cancel.cancel()`, so SSE streams stay open for the duration of the checkpoint before all terminating together; `src/main.rs` runs `optimize_database` again once `server::main` returns.

The server tests boot the real `server::main` against a real listener and drive it over HTTP with reqwest, each file on its own port (8000-8003, 8010 mutations, 8011 queries, 8012 uploads) serialised by the test-only `config::MUTEX`; they are timing-based — sleep, then assert through GraphQL — so they cover the queue-and-notify contract, the DataLoader edges and the size aggregates, the status-code contract, and validator rejection surfacing as a GraphQL `errors` array rather than a panic. The query test now pins that `dependencies` lists both `chd-rs` and `sevenz-rust2` (linked-in engines that always report `built-in`) and that the list is sorted by name, rather than expecting a null version for a missing tool.

`QueryRoot.dependencies` reports eight format engines sorted by name — `sevenz-rust2`, `chd-rs`, `ctrtool`, `xps-rs`, `xso-rs`, `nsz-rs`, `xdelta-rs` and `nod` (which also backs WBFS) — and only `ctrtool` can be absent: every other module's `get_version()` returns the literal `built-in` and never fails (`nsz-rs` adds `, prod.keys not found` when the Switch key file is missing), while `ctrtool` is spawned through `tool_version` so its GraphQL `version` is `null` exactly when the binary is not on `PATH`. The same list is reused by `oxyromon info` and the MCP read tool, and CIA import re-checks `ctrtool` itself rather than trusting the report.

`systemSettings(systemId)` returns the effective configuration rather than a row lookup: it loads the global settings and that system's overrides, merges them by key with the override winning, and sorts by key — so a client reading `settings` alone would display defaults the system has already overridden.

The read surface has no filtering or search beyond its declared arguments: `systems`, `games(systemId, offset, limit)` and `roms(gameId)` return rows ordered by name with no completion, region or status filter, while `version`, `dependencies` and `gameInformation(gameName)` resolve entirely without the database — `gameInformation` parses a No-Intro name in-process and `downloadableSystems(update)` only filters the built-in Redump catalogue against the systems already imported.
